web_title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: Inside Every Segment — Products, Customers & Real-World Examples
question: What does PDS Limited actually sell, how much does each segment contribute to revenue and profit, and how does a real-world order flow from sketch to store?

epigraph.quote: A great sourcing platform is invisible to the shopper, indispensable to the retailer's buyer, and relentless on the factory floor.
epigraph.author: Global Apparel Supply Chain Note

web_blocks.title: Segment Revenue & Profit Architecture: Sourcing Dominates, Manufacturing Adds Margin

web_blocks.html: PDS organizes its ₹13,110 Cr FY26 (₹7,876 Cr H1 FY27) business into three segments: Sourcing, Manufacturing, and Others [4, 5, 11]. Sourcing drives ~94%–95% of revenue and most of the EBIT. Manufacturing adds ~5%–6% of revenue at higher margins (5.8% EBIT in H1 FY27 vs. 2.3% for Sourcing) [11, 12]. Others holds brand management and ventures.

web_blocks.takeaway: Sourcing drives 94%+ of scale at a ~2.3% EBIT margin; Manufacturing earns higher margins (5.8%) on a small base; 'Others' remains a drag due to Ted Baker's ₹11 Cr H1 FY27 loss.

web_blocks.title: Segment 1: Design-Led Sourcing & Sourcing-as-a-Service (94%+ of Revenue)

web_blocks.html: Within Sourcing, PDS runs two commercial models. The core engine is Design-Led Sourcing (DLS). In-house designers in London, Hong Kong, New York, and Mumbai create seasonal collections and develop samples. PDS then sources fabrics and allocates production across 600+ partner factories in Bangladesh, China, Turkey, India, and Vietnam. It delivers finished garments to Primark, Tesco, Sainsbury's, Asda, Next, Walmart, Target, and Kohl's [4, 6, 11]. The top 10 verticals generate ~75% of revenue, led by flagship UK unit Poeticgem [11, 13].

The second model is Sourcing-as-a-Service (SaaS), launched in FY22 [13]. Under SaaS, PDS does not buy fabric or hold inventory title. Instead, large retailers outsource their regional buying desk to PDS for a fixed fee plus a commission on Gross Merchandise Value (GMV) [13, 14]. PDS tracks both GMV (₹5,146 Cr in Q1 FY27) and statutory revenue. Roughly 70% of GMV converts to reported revenue, while SaaS fees carry minimal working capital [13, 15].

web_blocks.title: Concrete Real-World Example — Segment 1 (Sourcing): How a UK Value Retailer Buys 500,000 Autumn Knitwear Pieces
paragraphs: Customer & Problem: A major UK retailer (such as Primark or Tesco F&F) needs 500,000 women's ribbed knit cardigans for Autumn/Winter. Shipments must land within 14 weeks at a £14 retail price, with zero compliance errors.

Product & Delivery: Six months ahead, PDS's London studio (Poeticgem) presents 40 trend samples. Once the buyer picks 12 SKUs, PDS locks yarn pricing and splits production across three audited factories in Gazipur, Bangladesh. PDS stations quality inspectors on the sewing floor and manages Delivered Duty Paid (DDP) UK logistics.

Pricing & Economics: PDS invoices on FOB or DDP terms (~£4.50–£5.50 per piece). It earns an ~18%–20% gross margin over factory cost and nets ~2.3%–3.5% operating margin after London design and finance costs [11, 13].

web_blocks.title: Segment 2: Manufacturing (~5.7% of Revenue, 5.8% EBIT Margin)

web_blocks.html: Started in FY17, Manufacturing gives buyers guaranteed capacity for complex or fast-turnaround orders. PDS owns plants in Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, plus the FY26 acquisition of Knit Gallery in Tiruppur, India [4, 11, 16]. In July 2026, it also formed a manufacturing partnership with Indonesia's Busana Apparel Group. Manufacturing posted ₹452 Cr in H1 FY27 revenue and ₹26 Cr EBIT (5.8% margin) as utilization rose [11].

web_blocks.title: Concrete Real-World Example — Segment 2 (Manufacturing): Knit Gallery & Busana Serving Duty-Sensitive US & EU Programs
paragraphs: Customer & Problem: A US retailer (such as Kohl's or Target) wants organic-cotton infantwear with full yarn-to-garment traceability outside China.

Product & Delivery: PDS routes the order to Knit Gallery in Tiruppur or Busana partner lines in Indonesia. Automated cutting, GOTS-certified dyeing, and high-speed knitting produce fully traceable garments under direct factory supervision.
Pricing & Economics: Capturing the factory conversion spread lifts segment EBIT to 5.8%—more than double pure sourcing's 2.3% margin, though with higher depreciation [4, 11].

web_blocks.html: In April 2023, PDS partnered with Authentic Brands Group (ABG) to run Ted Baker Design Group (via UK unit New Lobster) [17, 18]. However, ABG's UK retail franchisee entered administration and US partner deals fell through. London overhead proved too heavy for wholesale-only sales. H1 FY27 income rose 30% YoY to ₹268 Cr (22% gross margin), yet New Lobster lost ₹11 Cr (down from ₹30 Cr prior year). Management placed the unit under strategic review in November 2026 [19]. Elsewhere, PDS Ventures holds small fashion-tech stakes whose M2M gains flow through Other Comprehensive Income [13].

web_blocks.title: Concrete Real-World Example — Segment 3 (Brand Management): Ted Baker Wholesale via New Lobster
paragraphs: Customer & Problem: UK and European retailers (such as John Lewis or Zalando) want Ted Baker menswear and dresses after its standalone UK store chain collapsed.

Product & Delivery: New Lobster designs the collection in London and sources it through PDS's Asian factories. It sells wholesale to B2B partners and pays royalties to Authentic Brands Group [18, 19].

Pricing & Economics: Wholesale gross margins hit ~22% in H1 FY27, but London corporate overheads exceeded gross profit by ₹11 Cr. Management is now evaluating cost relocation, partnerships, or an exit within FY27 [19].

web_blocks.title: Geographic Mix & Customer Concentration: UK/EU Anchor vs. Americas Surge

web_blocks.html: Europe and the UK remain PDS's foundational profit pool, generating roughly two-thirds of consolidated GMV. Anchor buyers include Primark, Tesco, Sainsbury's, Asda, and Next [4, 11, 13]. However, North America (Americas) is now the fastest-growing engine. Americas revenue jumped +44% YoY in H1 FY27 and +54% YoY in Q2 FY27. Seven of the top ten US retailers have moved from trial capsules into core seasonal orders [4, 15]. Meanwhile, the top 10 verticals drive ~75% of revenue alongside 40+ emerging verticals [11, 13].

Investors often ask why Design-Led Sourcing earns ~18%–20% gross margin when Indian buying agents charge just 2%–3% [11, 13]. The difference is principal ownership versus brokerage. PDS designs garments in London, buys fabric, manages DDP logistics, and invoices the finished product. Design payroll and finance costs sit inside SG&A, leaving a 2.3%–3.5% operating margin [11, 13]. By contrast, SaaS bills pure fees and commissions with minimal inventory [13, 14].

Category diversification also cushions PDS against single-trend fashion swings [1, 11]. Its core lines span women's wear, men's wear, children's wear, and everyday essentials [1]. Essentials and basics—such as multipack tees, socks, loungewear, and kids' knitwear—make up a large share of supermarket volumes at Tesco, Asda, and Primark [1, 11]. Retailers reorder these staples every quarter regardless of high-fashion trends. Meanwhile, PDS has added newer verticals in activewear, home textiles, and beauty packaging [11, 13]. In Manufacturing, Knit Gallery in Tiruppur adds specialized circular-knitting capacity for infantwear and organic cotton [16]. Paired with Busana in Indonesia, PDS can now offer buyers both asset-light sourcing speed and dedicated factory capacity for duty-sensitive US programs [4, 16].

book_paragraphs: If you walk into a Primark on Oxford Street in London, a Tesco superstore in Manchester, or a Kohl's in suburban Ohio and pick up a £14 ribbed cardigan or a $24 cotton polo, there is a meaningful chance PDS Limited put it on the hanger. Yet you will never see the PDS name on the neck label. To understand how a ₹13,110 crore business operates behind the scenes, let's break down its three engines and walk through an actual garment's journey in each.

The first—and by far the largest—engine is Design-Led Sourcing, which accounts for roughly 94% of PDS's revenue. Think of PDS's London and Hong Kong showrooms as outsourced product-development departments for Western retailers. A buyer at a European supermarket chain does not have the bandwidth to fly to Dhaka, Tiruppur, and Guangzhou every month to chase 600 factories. Instead, PDS's vertical teams—like its flagship UK unit Poeticgem, which aspires to reach $1 billion in GMV on its own—present finished, trend-tested garment samples six months before the season. Once the retailer signs off on twelve styles out of forty samples, PDS locks yarn pricing, splits the 500,000-piece run across audited partner factories in Bangladesh to capture zero-duty UK market access, stations its own quality inspectors on the sewing floor, and handles customs clearance right up to the retailer's distribution center. For that end-to-end orchestration, PDS earns roughly an 18% to 20% gross margin over factory cost and nets a 2.3% segment EBIT margin on massive volume.

book_subsections.title: Sourcing-as-a-Service (SaaS): Turning Fixed Buying Offices into Fee Income
paragraphs: Layered onto traditional design-led sourcing is Sourcing-as-a-Service, or SaaS—launched in FY22 for mega-retailers that want PDS to run their regional buying desk for a management fee and GMV commission without PDS taking inventory title. That distinction explains why PDS reports both Gross Merchandise Value (₹5,146 crore in Q1 FY27 alone) and statutory revenue: roughly 70% of GMV converts into reported revenue, while pure SaaS fee mandates carry minimal working capital and higher net margins.

For a European supermarket chain or a French global hypermarket, maintaining a 40-person sourcing office in Dhaka or Shanghai carries heavy fixed payroll and compliance liability. By handing that mandate to PDS on a multi-year contract, the retailer converts fixed overhead into a variable percentage of shipped volume, while PDS gains multi-year visibility and higher return on capital.

book_subsections.title: Why Design-Led Sourcing Earns 18%–20% Gross Margins While Pure Agents Earn 2%–3%
paragraphs: When you first look at PDS's income statement, one line can puzzle newcomers: how does a sourcing intermediary report an 18% to 20% gross margin when traditional buying agents in Tiruppur or Dhaka charge a flat 2% to 3% commission? The answer lies in who owns the design and who invoices the garment.

A pure commission agent simply introduces a buyer to a factory and collects a 2% brokerage fee. By contrast, in PDS's Design-Led Sourcing model, PDS's London, New York, and Hong Kong teams originate the garment designs, buy the fabric, coordinate washing and testing across 600+ partner factories, clear customs, and deliver the finished carton directly to the retailer's distribution warehouse on Delivered Duty Paid terms. Because PDS takes legal title to the goods in transit and employs hundreds of Western designers and merchandisers, its gross margin looks like a wholesale brand's—18% to 20%—before London studio salaries, sampling, and trade-finance costs bring the net operating margin back down to 2.3%–3.5%.

book_subsections.title: Geographic Mix: From UK/EU Value Anchor to North American Growth
paragraphs: Looking at the map of PDS's customers reveals a classic two-speed engine. Historically, Europe and the United Kingdom have been PDS's bedrock, generating roughly two-thirds of total volume through entrenched relationships with value-fashion chains and supermarkets like Primark, Tesco, Asda, Sainsbury's, and Next. That UK/EU anchor provides steady, repeatable basics and knitwear replenishment even when discretionary fashion slows.

The second speed is North America, where PDS spent three years investing ahead of revenue to crack Tier-1 US retail accounts. Today, seven of the top ten US retailers are active customers, driving a +44% surge in Americas revenue during H1 FY27 and +54% in Q2 FY27. Because US retailers buy in larger single-SKU program sizes than fragmented European chains, sustained US scaling is the single biggest lever for lifting PDS's consolidated operating margin over the next two years.

book_subsections.title: Owned Manufacturing & The Ted Baker Cautionary Tale
paragraphs: The second engine is Manufacturing—about 5.7% of revenue (₹452 crore in H1 FY27), yet earning a 5.8% EBIT margin, more than double the sourcing segment's margin. Started in FY17 to guarantee capacity for complex or fast-turnaround orders, this arm operates plants in Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, reinforced by the FY26 acquisition of Knit Gallery in Tiruppur, India, and a July 2026 strategic partnership with Indonesia's Busana Apparel Group. When a US retailer like Target or Kohl's demands 100% yarn-to-garment traceability outside China, PDS routes those organic-cotton or activewear programs into its own Knit Gallery or Busana lines, capturing the full factory conversion spread.

Finally, there is the 'Others' bucket, dominated by the Ted Baker European wholesale operation (New Lobster) alongside PDS Ventures' startup stakes. That experiment has been a sobering lesson for both management and shareholders. When Authentic Brands Group tapped PDS in April 2023 to run Ted Baker's design and European wholesale hub, the thesis assumed a healthy UK and US retail-store franchisee network would anchor agency income. Instead, ABG's UK retail franchisee collapsed into administration and US opportunities evaporated. Even though B2B wholesale revenue grew 30% to ₹268 crore at a 22% gross margin in H1 FY27, the central London overhead still produced an ₹11 crore half-year loss—prompting management in November 2026 to place the unit under formal strategic review for restructuring, partnership, or exit.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Why Thin Margins Are a Feature—Until They Aren't
book_callouts.text: A 2.3% sourcing EBIT margin looks fragile at first glance, but when paired with negative working capital and minimal fixed assets, it can generate high returns on invested capital. The danger arises when a sourcing company steps up the risk curve into brand licensing—like Ted Baker—where fixed London overheads and inventory risk can quickly eat into the thin profits earned by the core sourcing engine.
